note: The School Trips uncertainty log (UK DfT TAG's term): one row per study a lever cites for an effect or a cost, graded for quality (Maryland Scientific Methods Scale for behaviour studies, FHWA CMF Clearinghouse stars for crash effects) and for fit (GRADE's four kinds of indirectness, EPA's benefit transfer size match), with whether its cost comes from the same program as its effect. documents lists cited sources that aren't studies (agency plans, budgets, datasets, news). Filled from the evidence notes in research/school-trips-2026-10/ on 2026-10-15; the grade-study skill (.claude/skills/grade-study/SKILL.md) adds a row. site/scripts/check-studies.mjs fails when a lever cites a study with no row.

studies.citation: Aldred, Croft and Goodman 2019, one-year evaluation of London's mini-Hollands programme
studies.use: One of three revealed-effect studies behind the 20% (10% to 30%) bike switch rate.
studies.design: Longitudinal controlled panel of 1,712 adults in high-dose mini-Holland areas against comparison areas, 2016 to 2017.

quality.smsWhy: The same people before and after, against a comparison group, not randomized, so level 3.
quality.cmfWhy: Not a crash study.

population.why: Adults in Outer London; the model's switchers are children's school trips.

intervention.why: A borough cycling programme, not a gap-free all-ages network to a school.

comparison.why: Comparison areas without the programme.

outcome.why: Cycled in the past week; car use showed only a non-significant downward trend.

transfer.studyEffect: 24% more likely to have cycled in the past week (95% CI 2% to 52%); 15.2% at control level against 22.4%
transfer.ourEffect: 20% of newly eligible driving students switch to bike, range 10% to 30%
transfer.ourExtent: driving students whose route newly passes the bike switch test
transfer.why: A relative rise in any past-week cycling among adults is not a share of drivers switching their daily school trip.

cost.why: Bike network costs come from SFMTA budgets.

studies.gaps: The About page says past-week cycling 'rose from 15.2% to 22.4% after a year', while the 2026-10-10 note gives 15.2% as the control level against 22.4% in high-dose areas, a comparison rather than a before and after change. The 2026-10-13 note read the abstract only.

studies.citation: Anderson, Hong and Jacobs, The Adoption-Substitution Gap, NBER Working Paper w29913, revised February 2026 (Sweden's 2018 national e-bike premium)
studies.use: Sets the e-bike vouchers' high of 640,000 car miles a year: 5,000 recipients at its upper bound of 205 km (127 miles) a year less driving each; the central 320,000 is the midpoint. In the School Trips model: Sets the low with Raleigh: recipients' car kilometres fell 1.4% to 3.9%, read as 3% of voucher families stop driving the school run.
studies.design: Odometer registry data on 89,621 recipients of a 25% premium up to SEK 10,000, against municipality trends.

quality.smsWhy: Recipients' odometer readings before and after against their municipality's trend, a comparison but not a lottery or matched control, so level 3.
quality.cmfWhy: Not a crash study.

population.why: Recipients were older and richer than average and 59% owned a car, mostly in smaller towns; SF's voucher is income-tested and about half of SF's EPC households are car-free.

intervention.why: An open 25% premium, not an income-tested $1,000 voucher by lottery.

comparison.why: Municipality trends, which the authors say make the figure an upper bound.

outcome.why: Car owners' odometer km; the scorecard applies 127 miles to all 5,000 recipients, car owners or not.

transfer.studyEffect: Car-owning recipients drove about 205 km (127 miles) a year less than trend, an upper bound
transfer.ourEffect: 640,000 car miles a year (127 x 5,000), central 320,000
transfer.ourExtent: all 5,000 SF voucher recipients
transfer.why: The scorecard applies a car owners' upper bound to every recipient; the equity note itself drops it to 90 miles once car-free households are counted.

cost.why: SF's voucher cost is $1,000 plus overhead, not Sweden's premium.

studies.gaps: The evidence note's read is carried from the What We Know doc ('per repo note'); not peer reviewed. The evidence note calls the design level 4; graded 3 here because only a municipality trend is described. Merged 2026-11-06 with the School Trips row: the 2026-10-13 lever-studies note links the same paper. The paper's after-trend range is 205 to 590 km a year, 1.4% to 3.9%, so 205 is the low end of that range, not a top.

studies.citation: Hoelscher, Salvo et al. 2025, STREETS study of Austin's bond-funded Safe Routes infrastructure, 64 infrastructure and 20 comparison schools
studies.use: Sets the safer crossings low case at 0 walk-and-bike points, and its about $400,000 a school sets the top of the cost range.
studies.design: Controlled serial cross-section, 11 waves of teacher hand tallies in grades 3 to 5, 2019 to 2024, 64 infrastructure schools against 20 comparison schools, results in conference slides.

quality.smsWhy: Repeated tallies at treated and comparison schools before and after works, not randomized, so level 3.
quality.cmfWhy: Not a crash study.

population.why: Grades 3 to 5 in Austin, baseline active share 14.3%, treated schools poorer than controls; SF TK-8.

intervention.why: Project types are not described in the slides read, so the match to bulbouts and beacons is unknown.

comparison.why: Schools without infrastructure works.

outcome.why: Active commuting trip counts, walk and bike only, no car outcome.

transfer.studyEffect: no gain through spring 2024; active trips fell during construction (estimates such as -150 trips, no interval)
transfer.ourEffect: the low case, 0 walk-and-bike points
transfer.studyExtent: works around each treated school, about $400,000 a school
transfer.ourExtent: every TK-8 school
transfer.why: Only the floor is taken, and the study's construction-period drag is not modelled.

Also graded in the injury pass: use Sets the floor of the safety upgrades' walking and biking gain at 0 (central 3.3 points from McDonald, high 6.3), because 64 schools with infrastructure showed no gain against 20 without; the model takes no injury figure from it, and its about $400,000 a school is the cost range's high. Gaps there: No peer-reviewed paper; only conference slides, unread in detail. No injury result is recorded in any note. The about page's cost text gives the range's ends as the walk audits and Monterey's $290,000, while the cost note sets $400,000 from STREETS; the two disagree on where the high comes from.

studies.citation: Boarnet et al. 2005, evaluation of California's Safe Routes to School construction program, 10 schools
studies.use: One of three revealed-effect studies behind the bike switch: a driving student newly within a safe ride as quick as the car switches to biking at 20% (10% to 30%).
studies.design: Parent survey after construction at 10 schools with a completed project, grades 3 to 5, comparing children whose usual route passed the project with those whose route did not, 39% response.

quality.smsWhy: A comparison group (route passes the project or not) with reported change since construction, but no before survey and a group that may not be comparable, so level 2.
quality.cmfWhy: Not a crash study.

intervention.why: Single construction projects, mostly for walking, not a connected all-ages bike network.

comparison.why: Children at the same schools whose route did not pass the project.

outcome.why: Any reported increase in walking or biking, not a daily switch from car to bike.

transfer.studyEffect: 15.4% (75 of 486) walked or biked more where the route passed the project, against 4.3% (16 of 376), a gap of 11.1 points of all children
transfer.ourEffect: 20% of newly eligible driving students switch to bike, range 10% to 30%
transfer.studyExtent: children whose route passed one project
transfer.ourExtent: driving students citywide whose route newly passes the bike switch test

cost.why: Bike network costs come from SFMTA budgets.

studies.gaps: The notes disagree on access: the 2026-10-10 note read the eScholarship copy's Table 2, while the 2026-10-13 note says the eScholarship copy returned nothing and read only the abstract. The 2026-10-12 review asked for Boarnet's decimals to be checked against the primary. The 2026-10-12 review recommended 5% (0% to 20%); the 2026-10-13 note and the model keep 20% (10% to 30%).

studies.design: Traffic over the charging line, before and after the charge.

quality.smsWhy: Before and after, with no comparison area.
quality.cmfWhy: Not a crash study.

intervention.why: A cordon charge, a close match to SF's, at a different price.

comparison.why: Stockholm before the charge.

outcome.why: Entries over the line, against SF citywide miles.

transfer.studyEffect: About 20% fewer entries
transfer.ourEffect: 33M to 112M miles a year citywide
transfer.ourExtent: Downtown SF cordon
transfer.why: SF's range isn't this effect; it comes from SFCTA's model and a carbon stand-in.

cost.why: SF's cost is its own estimate.

studies.gaps: Graded from the repo's notes, not from the study opened in this pass.

quality.cmfWhy: Not a crash effect, so no Clearinghouse rating applies.

comparison.why: No comparison.

outcome.why: Stated car use, described in words, with purchase as owning, ordering or planning combined.

transfer.studyEffect: car use drops at two weeks, increases again by six months; 62% owning, ordering or planning to buy

studies.citation: Cervero 2006, Transit-oriented development's ridership bonus, UC Berkeley working paper
studies.use: Sets family homes' 9.8 miles a day: 226 California movers with the same job went from 33.3 to 23.5 commute miles.

quality.cmfWhy: Not a crash study.

population.why: People who chose to move near rail, against families in new SF homes.

intervention.why: No study of this method: moving near rail, not funding family homes.

comparison.why: No comparison group.

outcome.why: Gross commute only, before new residents' own driving.

transfer.studyEffect: 33.3 to 23.5 commute miles a day, recalled
transfer.ourEffect: 0 to 2.3M miles a year
transfer.ourExtent: 2,930 homes, about 1,050 workers who now commute in
transfer.why: A fall measured on one group of movers, borrowed for a group nobody has followed.

studies.citation: Chizeck and Mbonu 2025, randomized trial of discounted and free transit fares, Pittsburgh
studies.use: Bounds the free caregiver fare at 1 Muni point (0 to 3) among TK-8 students over half a mile: free fares cut adults' daily chance of a car trip 2.9 points, trips with children did not change, and the half-fare arm moved nothing.
studies.design: Randomized trial of no discount, half fare or free fare for 16 to 19 months, 9,544 low-income SNAP adults and 4,928 children aged 6 to 17.

quality.smsWhy: Fare levels randomized across participants, so level 5.
quality.cmfWhy: Not a crash study.

population.why: Low-income SNAP adults in a less dense city; SF caregivers of TK-8 students.

intervention.why: A free fare for all of an adult's trips, where children in Pittsburgh pay; in SF children already ride free, so the lever frees only the caregiver's fare on school trips.

comparison.why: Randomized control at full fare.

outcome.why: Daily chance of any car trip; the model needs Muni share on school trips and takes 88% of new riders from single-family cars by its own split.

transfer.studyEffect: daily chance of a car trip down 2.9 points (SE 1.1) from 34.6%; trips with children -0.136 (SE 0.124) from 1.46; GPS car trips a week -1.67 (SE 1.44), interval includes zero
transfer.ourEffect: 1 Muni point, range 0 to 3, among TK-8 students over half a mile, 88% from cars
transfer.ourExtent: school trips of about every TK-8 student over half a mile, citywide
transfer.why: The 1 point is a judgment set below Pittsburgh's figure because trips with children did not move; Pittsburgh's 2.9 on a 34.6% base would be about 4.5 on SF's 55%, above the model's top.

cost.why: The $860 a rider comes from Muni's own fares, not from the trial.

studies.gaps: The 88% car share of new riders is the model's own split, and Litman puts 10% to 50% of added transit trips as car substitutes. The sim's CHANGES still applies a different rule (21% cost share times 50% take-up within 15 minutes), so the sim and the page do not share one rule. No study measures caregiver school trips under free fares.

studies.citation: Comandon and Boarnet 2025, Gas taxes, distance-based charges, and transportation network company charges, policy brief for the California Air Resources Board (citing the Dimitropoulos et al. 2018 meta-analysis of 74 studies)
studies.use: Its per-mile cost elasticity of miles driven, -0.10 to -0.12 (Dimitropoulos), and per-mile pilot elasticities of -0.13 to -0.18 set the low end of the -0.1 to -0.3 range behind the 5-cent charge's 1% to 8% driving cut and so its 37 to 300 people hurt avoided a year.
studies.design: A review: a meta-analysis of 74 studies of the cost of driving per mile, plus volunteer per-mile pilots (Puget Sound 275 households, Melbourne 1,400, Switzerland 3,700) whose control groups the brief doesn't describe.

quality.smsWhy: The meta-analysis pools mostly observational price-response estimates with no comparison group, and the brief doesn't describe the pilots' controls, so level 2.
quality.cmfWhy: Not a crash study; the injury figure assumes injuries fall in step with miles.

population.why: Drivers in many countries and volunteer pilot households; SF drivers on SF streets.

intervention.why: Fuel prices and voluntary per-mile accounts; a mandatory 5-cent SF rate on a state meter that doesn't exist.

comparison.why: Price variation over time and across places, not a charged against an uncharged group.

outcome.why: Miles driven; the scorecard figure is people hurt, which the note assumes falls in step with miles, and it says faster traffic could make crashes more severe.

transfer.studyEffect: Elasticity of miles to per-mile cost -0.10 to -0.12 (74 studies); per-mile pilots -0.13 to -0.18; 'a 10% increase in the charge results in a 1% to 2% decrease in VMT'
transfer.ourEffect: 5 cents a mile (9% of $0.56 running cost, or about a quarter of fuel cost) at -0.1 to -0.3 cuts SF driving 1% to 8%, so 37 to 300 of about 3,720 people hurt a year
transfer.studyExtent: household driving under fuel prices or a pilot account
transfer.ourExtent: every SF street, all drivers
transfer.why: The elasticity is in the right unit for miles, but the high end (-0.3 on fuel cost) comes from a Stockholm model parameter, not this review, and the injury step is an assumption.

cost.why: The $6M to $16M running cost is 5% to 10% of revenue from the SB 339 analysis, not the cost of the pilots reviewed.

test.low: -0.1 on 9% of running cost: 1% less driving, 37 hurt avoided
test.high: -0.3 on about a quarter of fuel cost: 8% less driving, 300 hurt avoided

studies.gaps: Dimitropoulos et al. 2018 and the pilot reports were not opened; the note tags them secondary through the brief. The road-pricing note found the Swiss figure the brief gives (-0.31) differs from the journal's -0.24 on external costs. The high elasticity of -0.3 is Stockholm's traffic model parameter (Borjesson et al. 2012, Table 2), listed in documents.

studies.citation: Comandon and Boarnet 2025, Impacts of Road Pricing on Passenger Vehicle Use and Greenhouse Gas Emissions, policy brief, USC for the California Air Resources Board
studies.use: Its 1% to 3% metro-wide CO2 fall from cordons, read as 1% to 3% of SF's 43.9% car share, sets the downtown charge's 0.4 to 1.3 citywide car share points (central 0.85).
studies.design: A review of before and after studies of cordon and area charges (Stockholm, Gothenburg, London, Singapore and others) and of toll elasticities; no new measurement.

quality.smsWhy: The metro-wide figure comes from before and after studies of charged cities with no comparison region, summarised in a review, so level 2.
quality.cmfWhy: Not a crash study.

population.why: Stockholm, London and other European metro areas with 60% to 65% transit shares to the centre; SF's downtown transit share was about 36% in 2023.

intervention.why: Entry cordons and area charges, the way the SF option proposes.

comparison.why: Before the charge, with no unpriced comparison region.

outcome.why: CO2 across a metro area, which the note carries over to the share of trips by car; the review itself finds 'a lack of evidence to link road charging with a region-wide reduction VMT'.

transfer.studyEffect: CO2 down 13% to 20% in the zone and 1% to 3% across the metro area
transfer.ourEffect: 0.4 to 1.3 points of SF citywide car share (1% to 3% of 43.9%), central 0.85
transfer.studyExtent: whole metro areas around charged central zones
transfer.ourExtent: all trips to, from and within SF, from one downtown cordon at $6.50 a peak entry
transfer.why: A metro emissions change is a different unit from a city's car share, and SF's lower transit share makes a smaller response likely, as the note itself says.

cost.why: The setup and running costs come from SFCTA's 2010 cordon estimate and New York's spending, not from the charges this review covers.

studies.gaps: The underlying studies behind the 1% to 3% were not opened; the brief's own citation for it is not recorded in the notes. No study measures a cordon's effect on a city's car share, so the CO2-to-car-share step is ours.

transfer.studyEffect: 536 unique requests from 157,000 students (0.34%), or 710 with siblings (0.45%); 27% still carpooling a year on
